title: I Took the Tea-Ceremony Room Booking to the Host Who Left My Numbered Chawan

parts.text: I stepped into the tea room at 10:02 a.m. and host Aiko was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE ROOM. FORTY MINUTES. CHAWAN STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-two, room secretary, holding a clipboard that listed our numbered chawan. Aiko shrugged. "Hosts are the room." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover whisk on my numbered chawan. Then I asked for the room log. At 10:10 the desk pinged why Aiko's name was on my whisk. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Aiko's leftover whisk on my numbered chawan.

social.video_title: She left my numbered chawan on my tea-room booking — Part 1/2
social.description: Tea room, leftover whisk, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the chawan. Would you have asked for the room log?

parts.text: Aiko called it temae until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the whisk still. The chawan went back to my numbered booking. Aiko ran a slot of her own and told the next host atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: HOSTS ARE NOT THE ROOM. I keep my chawan on a labeled shelf. Aiko brown-bags her temae. The tea room finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Hosts are not the room — Part 2/2
social.description: Room log, numbered chawan, and a second line on the board. Was temae ever my whisk?
